Show your dog a treat or his favorite toy, and then place it out of his sight but easily accessible. Tell him to “Find it!”. Once he finds it praise enthusiastically. You can start to increase the difficulty of the game by turning off the lights, adding more treats, using boxes or even hiding treats in less conventional places like inside of a shoe. The rewards for the dog are multiple- he gets a treat or finds his toy plus a very happy handler. If issuing a toy, be sure to reward his find with some play before starting again. When multiple treats or toys are used, this particular game helps to build persistence and trust in the handler. The dog may initially find only 2 out of 3 treats, but he quickly discovers that persistence in searching when you give the “Find it!” cue pays off. He learns to believe you - there really is another one there! FreeworkIntroduction to FreeworkPlace snuffle mats and licky mats around an rea of your hours and load them with treats, yogurt, peanut butter, etc… Let your dog go in and explore the area while enjoying the amazing treats you set out for him. This game allows your dog to freely go in an area and explore. Also create a list of real-life rewards that he will work for (meal time, access to a snuffle mat, opening a door, etc). Utilize those cues to give him explicit permission to access something he wants and change it up every time. This will teach Theo to slow down, listen to your request and work for what he wants. 8/10/2025 Approached Stav (Rama) from inside portion of his run. He presented with barrier reactivity. I let him go out to the outside portion of the run. He would occasionally come up to the gate to see what I was doing but then immediately retracted to the back of the kennel. He would low growl with whale eyes if I turned around. Realizing that he was more scared then anything, I cracked the run door open to see if he would approach. As soon as the run door opened and I offered my hand for a sniff, he approached me with a low-wagging tail. I offered him my leash to which he lowered his head and allowed me to put it on. Exited the kennel and walked to the mulch yard. When we got into the mulch yard, I let him roam around (with the leash still on). I sat on the bench and allowed him to approach me if he wanted. I observed that he was heavily panting due to stress. However, he would approach me with a wagging tail and allow me to pet his head and back. We left the mulch yard and went for a walk to the next yard over where he did a fence greeting with Bubba Boy. He seemed excited to meet another dog and I suspect he is dog friendly. We then walked inside and I brought him over to the supervisor desk. He stopped midway to greet two customers in which he offered submissive ears and a tail wag. Once at the desk, he was met by a few kennel techs. While he did show some shyness, he allowed one kennel tech to pet his head. We went back to 200, I placed him back in his kennel and unleashed without incident. Recommend L3-SF and a playgroup assessment.

She is very hungry for human attention, she wags her tail and gives them a smile to let them know she's ready for pets, and people have only gently approached her and she loves to let them pet her. She's very gentle and affectionate with humans.What does this dog do when you or someone else goes near the food bowl while they are eating? If we walked by too close to the dog bowl she'd look a little distracted and look to what we were doing, but didn't seem protective or anything.What does this dog do when someone tries to take away toys, bones, food, or anything the dog decides is valuable? She protects them and nips a little bit and jumps if you pick it up and don't immediately throw or drop it.What does this dog do when someone tells them to get off of furniture? She is usually responsive and obedient, unless she was really sleepy it would take her some coaxing to get down. It also hurt her leg to jump down, so if she wasn't doing it on her on accord, she was a little hesitant. She LOVES to sleep on the couch.What is this dog's best quality? Friendly, gently affectionateWhat is this dog's worst quality? Injured, lack of trainingCheck all that apply to this dog's personality: Friendly, Shy, Clingy, Goofy, Polite, Fearful, AffectionateIn your own words, describe this dog's personality Puma is genuinely the sweetest dog I've ever known. She stole our hearts immediately on meeting her and we loved her more by the minute. She was shy upon meeting her, and continued to be very gentle and clingy. She's very affectionate to everyone she sees, wagging her tail and giving a smile that lets you know she'd like some pets. She loves to be near her humans, and will whimper if she doesn't have access to them. She is a low energy dog, which might be due to her injury, but she very rarely wanted to run around and be active, rather her favorite thing to do was nap on the couch in whichever room we were in. She was cuddly and wanted to be touching her humans, but she would not beg for attention, she just really welcomed it and you could tell she felt safest when she was close and getting gentle pets. She would bark when scared or curious, but not overboard and would normally stop if we asked her to. For example, she is protective of her house and would bark at neighbors and folks approaching/passing the house pretty gently through the fence or the window, and when in the crate at night.With a little more crate and command training, and lots of support for her injury, she'll be a perfect dog for someone who wants a chill, sweet, human-loving companion.What is this dog afraid of? How do they react? She gets shy, cowers her head, sometimes gets a little shaky. We saw this when she was getting used to a new spot in the house, and when she was in the car. And if she is consistently scared (in the crate) she cries/whimpers. She did this thing where she would slowly backpedal and walk sideways or in circles when getting through certain thresholds in the house - a hallway to the rooms in the house, between her crate and a wall to get to the kitchen, around the kitchen island. We thought at first perhaps it was due to her injury, but it seemed like it was derived more from fear, and then once she spun through that spot she'd do a little gallop and speed up like she was proud to have gotten through the scary part. Otherwise, she didn't like loud noises / appliances very much. She hated the vacuum and would immediately bark and try to take it from our hands / nip at it, same with a lawn mower we were assembling. Regular noises didn't bother her much, but sudden loud ones were not welcome.All dogs have sensitive places She didn't like to be touched on her injured paws/legs, but otherwise didn't notice any reactions. When touching those areas, to dry her off after being in the rain, she would pull them back and look at you but not aggressively, and she'd still let you do it gently.Have you seen them act aggressively toward anyone? NoPlease tell us anything you would like us to know about this dog to help us find it an adoptive home I think I covered it mostly in the previous sections, but she should be in a home where folks are home often and can pay attention to her needs (or gradually train her to be comfy being home alone), and one that is prepared to train her on more commands, and most importantly help her recover safely from her injury. When walking her, she needs to be on a secure harness. She is sweet, gentle, loving, sleepy and lower energy, smelly-treat-motivated, a little goofy, clingy, and an all around wonderful young adult dog who deserves a happy home.Though we don't have experience with her being in a house with children and other dogs, we think given the personality traits she showed and with training that those could be possibilities. Given her desire to play with prey outside, she probably wouldn't do well in a house with cats. She was very well house trained and I would completely trust her to roam free in the house if we were sleeping and weren't home, but we wanted to start crate training her since she'll need to be restricted and get used to that during her surgery recovery. She didn't have any accidents, and was good at telling us when she needed to go outside and picked a spot in the yard to do her business consistently.Puma will light up and bring peace to your days, and you will not regret loving and letting this sweet angel love you.Would you like to be notified if this animal is ever at risk for euthanasia? Later went by to visit him while out in the play yard. He was loose and wiggly at the gate, ignored treats but did allow us to come into the yard. Had zoomies and tried to jump a few times but redirected easily with a "sit" command or back turning. Knows sit, lay down and paw. Brought into the office to dress for DFTD 15 minutes later and he was quickly amped up coming into the office. Pulling, jerking on the leash, heavily stress panting, increasing overarousal. Lynn had to hold the leash firmly and give him several minutes to calm down in order to put the harness and collar on. Incredibly frustrated and pent up with energy. The DFTD was comfortable with taking a hard puller on leash and energetic dog for a trail walk (limited visual on other dogs) so we decided he needed to get out of the kennel for a bit. He did not mouth or bite at any point in the interactions, just very jumpy with high energy spins. Use treats to retrieve from kennel and monitor barrier reactivity. BR observed and level of OA in office is notably concerning. Currently leveled as a L2-OA/JM. Including BR in level.

8/21/2025 8/21/25Hi there,Here are notes about Whiskey during this week-long evaluation.  We can keep him for a few more days, possibly returning him on Sunday or Monday - still working on the logistics as we will be traveling next week and I know Tuesdays are rough and I want to continue to set him up for success as much as possible.Home set-up:Whiskey was housed in a separate room, away from our 2 resident dogs.  The room is double gated at the door - a baby gate at the threshold and a removable gate to add more distance from my resident dog's noisy eyes to the entrance of the room.  The room is on the third floor of our townhome and was set-up with cameras for additional monitoring.  The loudest the room would get would be when I was home and on work calls.  We also had an air filter running all day, on it's highest setting it can be loud, but seemed like white noise.When Whiskey needed to go out/downstairs for a walk or to go potty, our 2 residents dogs were crated and secured in a space on the main floor where Whiskey could not approach their gates directly.  The ground floor is my husband's space and where he works.  We practiced crate and rotate in our home while Whiskey was with us.Daily routine:Whiskey was taken out 3-4 times a day, depending if I went to the office.  Frequent breaks ensured he did not go potty in the house.  When at home, one of those outings would be a lunch-time or early afternoon 10-15 minute walk outside.  Whiskey was fed 2x a day, breakfast and dinner.  When working from home, I would crate him after breakfast and after his lunch-time walk, I would have him roam the room free while I continued to work. After dinner, I let Whiskey have the room on his own, uncrated.  He usually just lay on the floor and watched the door until I came back.  He would be crated overnight as he slept.Health notes:Whiskey still coughs, but there are no signs of phlegm and his nose is no longer runny/mucus-y.  His coughs happen mostly when he has just woken up or when he's walking up and down the stairs.  He is still taking doxy in the AM along with his breakfast.  He is still butt scoots on occasion.  His nose and paws are very dry though, they feel scratchy. Pus still continues to show up around his eyes, though not as much as when he first got here - but still present.  He seems to have some stiffness in his rear legs though.Eyesight:I think Whiskey can see shadows, the bigger the item the better he can maneuver around it or at least know that it's there.  He still walks down steps tentatively, but I've noticed that he prefers to walk along the stair wall, I'm assuming it helps him navigate.  He also seems to navigate better in bright light vs. a dark room.I don't know if it's eyesight or spatial distancing might be his issue or both, but sometimes he will run right into me in the backyard because he didn't realize I was right there.  He often missteps when coming to a curb. He may also flinch when you pet him on the head or under his chin because he didn't see your hand coming.General behavior:Talking - When he does make a sound, he roos or makes deep vocal grunts.  It can sound growly, but as you get to know him, it's not a growl or at least not a warning one.  He's usually vocal when we are outside or when I'm with him upstairs and playing with him and his toys.On-leash - He can pull, but he's getting better at not pulling too hard.  When he pulls, it's because something got his attention, curiosity, or interest.  Dogs walking (or barking), people walking by, strollers nearby, cats, etc.Leash-biting - Only showed leash biting when we swapped leash to a slip lead vs. leash with a clasp to his collar.  He initially attempted leash biting when you try to put the slip lead over his head. If you dangle the other end of the leash in front of him, he has tried to grab it.  To curb this, we've sprayed the slip lead with bitter apple spray and also use special treats to reward him when we can put on/take off the leash with minimal to none LB behavior.  We have also rewarded him when he lets go of the leash, if he was able to get a hold of it.  I have noticed that when the slip lead is loop is big enough where it can go over his head without him touching it on the sides of his face, it is easier and quicker to get the leash on.Potty-trained:  Whiskey is potty-trained, though it may take a few days for him to learn where he can go.  We aim to have him go out 4x a day to prevent any accidents, though 3x a day can also work where he was taken out in the morning, when I got home from work, and before going to bed.Crate-trained:  Whiskey does well in a crate and has learned to go inside on his own by tapping on the top of the crate.  Since the time he's been with us, he's only barked once in the crate, and that was during a thunderstorm. He only barked once and then was able to settle.  As he got healthier/felt safer, he midly whines when he is in the crate but still sees you near. It's more of a muffled whine, but he does not do it long and then just lays down in the crate to sleep.Treats - Whiskey is a gentle treat taker, because of his sight issues, he may need a visual cue to listen to where the treat is.  The best treats for him are smelly ones.Interactions:Other people in the home/men:  He has responded well to my husband who has given Whiskey pets and treats. My husband would come up to the baby gate where Whiskey would come up and seek pets.  Whiskey would also go up to my husband on his own when my husband was at his desk to seek pets.Kids:  We have not had him directly near kids or interact with kids.  The closest to a kid he has been was walking by the community pool on a weekend.  These were mostly small/younger kids, but a few were screaming very loudly that it made Whiskey anxious.  He pulled me towards the pool gate and attempted to try to put his head through the fence. I'm not sure if he had the intention to go through the fence or if he just couldn't tell/see a fence existed.Cats: We bumped into a neighborhood cat who was more scared of  Whiskey than Whiskey was of the cat.  Whiskey showed some interest, but I was able to call him towards me before we continued our walk.Dogs:  Both resident dogs seem curious about Whiskey, but we did not allow any type of meet and greet or walks together.  Reese (our female dog) would watch him through the baby gate+secondary gate.  When he knows she's there he will go over to the doorway.  On the second day, it seemed like he was about to make an attempt to jump on the baby gate to get a better look at Reese, but I told him "no" and got him to go back into his crate.  He hasn't tried it since.Toys and things:  Whiskey seems to prefer crinkly type toys the best, though eh has been caught licking or mouthing at sheets/towels we used to catch any potty accidents.  He's not tearing or destroying anything, just lightly mouthing/nibbling.Suggestions:If Whiskey is unable to find placement out of the shelter, it's unclear if he will regress/decline once he's back at the shelter. Considering his stressors, this could be highlly likely.  If possible, he may do well in one of the flex rooms as they have more room and tend to be a lot quieter than the runs.

8/2/2025 Evaluate for placement options.8/4 Focus Group: I approached Cambria from the inside portion of her kennel. Her guillotine door was open so she immediately retreated outside. I tossed in a few treats and tried to call her inside. She was uninterested in treats and would not come inside. I then closed the door and approached her from the outside portion of her kennel. At this point kennel tech Ashley told me that kennel tech Heather was having issues with her body handling and her biting. I opened the run door and tossed in a few treats. At this point she retreated to the middle area of the outside run and was trying to hid. I slowly entered the run and sat down next to her. She had whale eyes and was shaking. I tossed her some more treats and talked to her. As she started to slowly shake less, I would move closer to her. When I got as close as I could to her, she stopped shaking all together. I offered my hand which she quickly sniffed and then turned around. She would avoid eye contact if it was silent but would make eye contact when I spoke to her. I offered her my leash and she turned and gave me whale eyes. I repeated these actions (offer hand, offer leash, talk to her, offer treats) for about 37 minutes. As soon as I felt she was calm enough to leash, I made the leash loop a bit bigger than she is and slowly slipped it over her head. I slowly tightened it and then slowly stoop up. She took a few seconds of coaxing to get her to walk with me. Once she started to follow me we walked toward the mulch yards. I allowed her sniff around on the grass and use the bathroom. We then walked over to the next grass area. As we were walking over there I noticed that she stayed close to me, almost under my feet close. We got to the second patch of grass and I again allowed her to sniff around. I then knelt down and called her over, she turned towards me but then turned away. At this point I slowly started to pet her back. I called her over again and this time she slowly approached me and allowed me to pet her head. We then walked back to her kennel. I walked into her kennel with her and she started to wag her tail. I knelt down again and she put her two front paws on my leg and allowed me to pet her head and body. I removed her purple collar that she had on, which she allowed with no issues and then I removed my leash with no issues. After the leash was removed she allowed me to pet her until her door opened to go back inside.

8/4/2025 Cambria was hiding in-between the guillotine and doggy door flaps when we approached her kennel. She ignored treats tossed into the kennel and already had a ton of uneaten treats around the kennel floor. We moved her to the inside kennel since the position she had in-between the doggy doors made it impossible to safely retrieve her. She walked over the inside without issue once the guillotine was lifted. I was able to leash her without incident but she did have whale eyes and was shaking. She walked without issue towards the play yards, sticking close to my feet. Once in the yard, she kept herself at a distance from Maddie and I so we just sat in the yard for awhile with her. She approached me without prompting after a few minutes and sniffed my hand. I praised her and reached to pet her but she lifted her lip. I decided to take her to a quite space to decompress for a few minutes and brought her to my office to roam while I entered FG notes. She spent most of the time under my desk, close to my feet.  Every few minutes she would venture out from under the desk to look out of the door and glance at me. I would praise her every time she came out and she started to give stronger tail wags each time. Once I finished entering notes, I stepped back from the desk and she came out from underneath slowly and approached me. She jumped up onto my lap and let me pet her. I got onto the floor with her and she crawled fully into my lap and licked my face and solicited attention all over. She took a step back after a few minutes and when I reached to pet her she lifted her lip and showed teeth. I slowly let my hand come closer to continue petting her and she stopped lip lifting to solicit attention instead. After some time in the office she started getting more confident and ran around the office to explore. She jumped into one of the unoccupied office chairs and spun around in it before jumping back down, shaking her whole body off then running up to me with a completely loose body and tail wags. She appears overall anxious and weary of strangers. She really needs to move out of 300 as she is terrified of the larger dogs in there and the noise. 

8/6/2025 Two potential adopters came in wanting a small female dog. Most of the ones in the shelter at the time were adopted so I talked to them about Cambria being a L3 SF and needing a lot of decompression time to see if they would want to meet her. I went to grab Cambria and she ran up to the gate to get leashed with a loose and wiggly body. She tried to jump into my arms but I placed her back down on the ground and showed the potential adopters that she is really sweet once she knows you. I brought her into the office to meet them in a quiet and controlled space. On the walk there she was a lot more confident on leash and didn't jump or shake like she did previously.  She approached a few people in the hallway to sniff but walked away before they could pet her. In the office, she oriented more around my feet and would glance at me to determine if it was safe to engage the adopters. She let them pet her and after a few minutes she slowly started approaching them and letting them pet her with more confidence. She was still hesitant to engage fully but made no attempts to bite and did not lip lift/show teeth as she has done in the past. 

8/13/2025 Starting to show SF to OA track behaviors. When attempting to put back in the kennel, she will jump and mouth all over my hands if she can reach them and nip at my ankles. This is the second time she has done this upon re-kenneling. Biting and chewing on the leash today and wouldn't let it go so I just dropped it and closed the kennel door. 

8/14/2025 Doing much better. Interacts with Volunteer, Hannah Sak, who may foster her. Greeting strangers with much less caution and fear. Wiggly and excited at the gate when she sees me. Handling interactions with strangers much better with reduced FAS observed. No longer as severe of a bite risk to others.-LNFirst on hand interaction with Cambria today other than just saying hello.  She ran up to the kennel door with loose body language and rubbed against the bars.  I opened the door and she was easily leashed.  When walking past people she was fine.  Jumped into my lap in the office and solicited affection.  Fine with BH.  Seemed happy and no SF seen in office.  Approving L2-SF because of her past history with fearfulness and anxiety.  -CW

Foster/Home Notes: 4/1/2025 PARCEL – 2 Week Foster Questionnaire 3/23 General Personality I want to preface this note. Parcel ended up with some respiratory issues and was fixed so he has spent most of his time quarantined from out other pets. This has also meant that we have not gotten out to do a lot of things that we would have at this point. I would like to update this after he gets to fully integrate in a few weeks. Parcel is an even tempered happy go lucky guy. He is pretty chill most of the time and will go with the flow. He enjoys being around and playing with other dogs, fine being around cats, curious, wants to be friends, just not sure how. Most of all, he really craves human attention. He will jump and be a bit mouthy at times when he really wants attention, but we are working on this. He is incredibly gentile taking treats, not a food or treat aggressive, fully crate trained, does well on a leash and loves to go on walks, he enjoys being outside in the back yard, but does not want to be left out on his own, rides well in the car, likes all people and is happy to get attention.Daily Routine He goes outside to the bathroom first thing, then eats and out again before a short walk in the morning. I will let him out a few times during the day as he is not fully housebroken. Around dinner time he gets fed again and will go out to do his business immediately after he eats. He goes on a second longer walk in the afternoon/evening.What food do they eat? Dry dog food and treats.What would be an ideal home and family for your foster? A family with time to give him lots of attention. I think he really likes having a "big brother" and some cat siblings and would do fine in a house with other pets, but he would also be happy to get all of the attention. After he recovers, we will spend time out hiking some of the local parks and see what he thinks about that and his energy level. My current dog never stops.On a scale of 1 to 5 how housetrained are they? 3Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts, or destruction? Fully crate trained. He may whine very briefly when you walk away, but does not bark or act out. He will willingly go in the crate when asked.Where do they sleep at night? Currently he is sleeping in a seperate room/crate while he recovers from respiratory illness and his recent castration. However, I think he would be very happy to sleep with the rest of us.Do they sleep through the night? YesHas he / she been exposed to any kids? If yes, what ages? How did it go? We will introduce him to kids when he is fully recovered from his respiratory issues. He did meet 2 middle school kids on his first day at the house and was very happy to get attention and was very calm.Has he / she been exposed to any cats? If yes, how did it go? Yes, we have 3 cats and his initial engagements were very positive. Parcel was mildly curious, but did not chase or even become excited. Of course, this is the same dog that does not chase squirrels. I'm not sure he is really a dog! (just kidding).Do they prefer men or women? No preferenceDoes he / she live with another dog? Yes, I have a 67 lb mix. They were very happy to play. A day after their introduction, Parcel showed signs of respiratory illness which has meant that he has had to be quarantined, but they are both anxious to get to play soon.Has he / she been around other dogs? Parcel seems to like other dogs and is very respectful when meeting a new friend and then will be playful. We will set up many more doggie play dates in the neighborhood once he recovers from his respiratory issues.Does he / she know any basic commands? Which ones (Sit, stay, come, lay down, etc) ? Yes, he knows some commands: stay, sit (when you are in front of him), and come (but he may not always obey). We are working on some additional training.Is your foster dog leash reactive? What makes them bark/lunge on leash? Overall, Parcel walks well on the leash, he does not bark at anything so far on a leash and the only time he has lunged is when he gets a great big mouthful of leaves/grass or might get spooked by a loud car/truck. He walks fairly well on the leash, but has started to test his limits and will pull some. We are working on learning heal.What devices do you use to walk your dog? (Type of harness, collar, etc) from the shelter he came with an elizabethen collar and a harness with an end of a leash attached to both. He does better with this setup than the collar alone. Still experimenting hereLeash Walking Rating 4How does your foster do in the car? He rides pretty well in the car. While he will not jump into the car, he does not fight being picked up and put in the car. I think this has to do with his avoidance of jumping on furniture in the house rather than something specific to the car. He rides in the back seat in a hammock, but he does at times want to come up to the front seat. He seems to enjoy going for rides, but we have not been on many at this time.How does your foster do for a bath? its not his favorite activity, but he will let you bathe him without a fight and he loves get toweled off!Energy level 3How much exercise does it take to tire them out? You can start doing this when he is heeling next to you and use a treat to lure him to turn to a different direction. Do this two or three times and then add your cue (like “This way”). Once he is doing this reliably start fading out the treat and only lure him with your empty hand and rewarding him with a treat at the end. Practice relaxation with low-value treats such as frozen peas. 3/4/2025 Foster reached out to me with the following message:Hey Fina, I have a behavior question for you regarding Whiskey. He went on trial adoption, but was returned to me after 4 days. They said he was too high energy and didn’t settle well in the evening, even though they felt like they had given him plenty of exercise. Their backyard set up ended up not being great because the fence wasn’t good and the dog Nextdoor was out and barked non stop. So when they walked him on their busy street, he got overstimulated. I think he didn’t have any time to really decompress there (he took a few day when he first came to me) and he never really settled in. They shared their concern about him barking and growling at them and “throwing a tantrum” when he didn’t get what he wanted, for example if he wanted to play while they were sitting on the couch. I’ve had him bark at me before in a play bow and try to jump up and get mouthy to elicit play or attention, but I have redirected him to a toy or left the room and the behavior stopped. I did tell them during the meet and greet about his mouthiness at times and the leash biting when overstimulated which has gotten much better, but it seems as this behavior came when he was frustrated with not getting something he wanted. I just got him back late last night and he is settling back in pretty well, but I’m wondering what I should do if this behavior continues. Any help would be appreciated! Thanks,Emily My email back:Hi Emily,I'm so sorry to hear that Whiskey's trial adoption didn’t work out. Please don’t feel discouraged—four days is not enough time for Whiskey to decompress, learn his new routine, and bond with new people.Sometimes, exercise doesn’t actually tire dogs out; instead, it can be like adding fuel to the fire. Have you ever taken a gym class, only to feel even more energized afterward and want to keep going? Exercise can have that same effect on both people and dogs. There could be many reasons why Whiskey had a hard time settling—it sounds like the combination of new people, a new environment, a barking dog, and a busy street may have overwhelmed him.The phrase "throwing a tantrum" concerns me. Whiskey isn’t trying to give them a hard time; he’s having a hard time and expressing his emotions the only way he knows how. Unfortunately, it can be difficult to get people to understand that behavior is just behavior—not evidence of dogs plotting against us (lol).I think ACE Freework could be really beneficial for Whiskey. This involves using snuffle mats and licking mats to encourage dogs to explore and engage their noses, which helps them calm down. Regularly practicing this will not only boost Whiskey’s confidence but also provide him with a safe space to explore without any pressure or expectations. The next family he visits can then use the same items in their home, offering Whiskey a sense of predictability and normalcy during the transition. I have a bit more information in this video: https://youtu.be/b1pImAsxRlw?si=aqITiFXnasrLmxLy. You can try some of the activities I mention and encourage the next family to do the same with Whiskey. For future placements, I also recommend that the next family have some frozen Kongs on hand. That way, if they’re relaxing on the couch and Whiskey wants to play, they can redirect him to a frozen Kong or a long-lasting chew while they unwind.I hope this is helpful! Please let me know how things go.Best regards,Fina Garcia

10/25/2023 A random car stopped with a random big dog hanging out the window barking, this person then got out of her car and approached the fosters yard with Marty on leash and her other two dogs in yard they all got really amped up and over stimulated  by the stranger and strange dog approaching to the point where the resident dog turned and redirected on Marty. Marty and the resident dog then latched on to one another, Marty was the only dog on leash, the foster struggled to keep them apart, but they kept latching, the neighbor came to help and was bit by Marty in the process of breaking up the dog fight. 

10/26/2023 10/25/23 I took Marty and my two dogs out to the yard. We have been keeping my one dog that he previously got into a fight with a Marty separate, but they have been doing better. So I took them outside and kept Marty on a leash in the yard to help him stay calm and work on boundaries. Everything was going well. Then someone I do not know parked in front of the fence and a large lab put its head out of the window and started barking in a bit of an aggressive way. My dogs reacted and ran up to the fence and started barking back. The owner then got out of the car and put the dog on a leash and brought it up to the fence. The lab dog was barking aggressively at my dogs, and they were getting very agitated. I kept Marty at a distance since he was on the leash. I called out to her and asked her to move away from the fence. She didn't really respond, and she looked like she was going to open the gate to come in. I then became scared she was going to enter, and I don't think she lives here so maybe she did not know the rules. I moved closer to try to get my dogs away from the fence. In his agitation my dog turned around and went for Marty and that is when they started fighting. I tried to get them apart, but they had latched onto each other's faces and wouldn't let go. A neighbor saw what was happening and he came into the yard and was trying to help me separate them. He managed to reach in and pull Marty's head back, but my dog was still trying to get to him. I think Marty was scared and in all the chaos he bit my neighbor's arm. I don't believe Marty intentionally bit my neighbor but was just in fight or flight mode. My neighbor went to the hospital, and I did get in contact, and they said the hospital notified animal control. I provided the vaccine records for both dogs. I asked for pictures of the injury, but they have not provided them so far. I was a bit alarmed to find out that Marty's rabies shots were not up to date. I am afraid that could put me in a very bad situation where I could face legal issues. I had just assumed all fosters would be up to date on vaccines. I know my neighbors were understandably upset and I offered to pay any medical expenses. I feel so horrible because I don't feel like it was completely Marty's fault so it will be devastating if his options are limited because of this. I don't think he is at risk of biting any people, but I do think he would be better off in a foster and home without other dogs or animals. I think with an experienced owner and training he would do very well, and he was already making great progress. So this is really heartbreaking, and I really am blaming myself. I think there is always a risk when you reach into a dog fight of getting bitten and I think that is what happened here.

She advised the leash was not fully on him and as she was trying to adjust the leash he started trying to fence fight with a neighboring dog and he kept turning like he was attempting to redirect.  I went to retrieve Jax roughly 5 minutes after this report was submitted. He was pawing at the door and did appear distressed (Observation Score a 3/5). I opened his kennel door and he jumped hard on the door a couple of times before he backed up and let me leash him. He came out of the kennel pretty strong and pulled hard on the leash. The dogs in his row were incredibly reactive and a couple were biting at their doors at him but he did not react. He sniffed a few and dipped into a few play bows before pulling on the leash to leave the room. Once out of the area I adjust the leash to sit just behind his ears and adjusted the leash into a figure 8 lock to provide some more support. He stopped pulled once the leash was adjusted. He was still pretty wiggly and excited on leash so I stood still long enough for him to lead into a sit next to me before walking. He pulled significantly less with the adjusted leash and was easily taken into the pathways office. I dropped the leash and let him sniff around. It was busy in the office with multiple volunteers and staff. He eagerly but gently took treats from Hannah and myself. He readily solicited attention from multiple people in the office and did not attempt to jump on anyone. I sat down to observe him further and see if he settled at any point. I noticed as more than one person tried to pet him he ducked and tucked his tail briefly with a panicked expression before loosening up again and going back to solicit attention. Everyone left the office and he settled and quietly explored the office. After a few minutes he began to pace anxiously and stress pant. Dr. D suddenly opened the office door and he jumped, startled and retreated briefly before loosening up again. I am observing some OA behaviors inside kennel and some levels of general anxiety/nervousness when out of the kennel. Again after the office cleared out he paced anxiously (tight smile, nervous pant, reddened eyes). He would periodically come back to my chair to solicit attention then pace the office again. His displayed overall quiet anxiety in the office and some overarousal/frustration when initially leaving the kennel. He pulled minimally when leaving the office but did look visibly more distressed once back in the hallway (tight smile returned, reddening around eyes). He was easily re-kenneled without issue. His behavior appears more anxiety driven than than anything, will revisit. He is currently a L1, moving him up to L2-OA/A. Recommending leash be adjusted into harness or adjust to leash to sit higher up when retrieving from his kennel.

6/22/2024 Very scared may come around. She was shaking and frozen. Startles easily, signs of fear/stress, and whale eyes.

6/26/2024 Very scared/reluctant to come up to the door but gave tail wags. Easily handled still a bit cautious around new people so go slow.

9/2/2024 Level down request. I have taken Firestar out twice recently, a week apart. Each time, she approached her kennel gate with relaxed body language and easily stepped into my leash loop. She did not hesitate through any thresholds, she approached me for attention. I didn’t notice any signs of shyness or fearfulness.

9/21/2024 She was a bit timid coming out of the kennel initially and meeting me but after a few sniffs and butt scratches she loosened up and got excited to leave the kennel. The dogs on the same wall side as her are very reactive and were biting at the gate doors, causing her to react briefly in turn and pull towards two kennels and snap at them. She was easily redirected by me calling to her and she pulled hard on leash towards the office. She ran and sniffed around the office for a few minutes before soliciting attention and jumping into my lap. I was able to pet her all over. She did not react when strangers entered the office but would alternate between soliciting attention/confidence from me, and pacing the office doors anxiously (worried eye brows, whining at the door.). If I got up to walk around, she followed closely behind me around the office. I can foresee some potential separation anxiety in a home but otherwise, she was easily handled, met strangers without displaying any concerning behavior or notable signs of fear and was confident walking on leash past non-reactive dogs. Recommending she level down from L2-SF to L1 with some anxiety, but can be handled by L1 volunteers and staff.  Notable Behavior: Some reactivity/brief fence fighting in response to other reactive dogs. Consider moving to another location to reduce in-kennel FAS.  Status Change/Recommendations: Level down from L2-SF to L1 and move to less reactive area.

1/31/2025 This was email communication to follow up of our meeting recap:Kayla:Thank you so much! We’ve already started working on a couple of the items! Her last park walk we sat at a gazebo that’s about 20 feet from the path and she was doing “auto check ins” even when we saw 4 dogs doing on leash greetings at the same time! I did have a question about potential adopter “meet and greets”. We have a family of 4 (one son in HS other college) wanting to meet her next weekend. I was thinking of actually having them come to our home and “anchor” them on our patio instead of doing it at a park which may be too busy and distracting.Then bring Katie May on to the patio, and instruct them to initially ignore her, don’t do strong eye contact, and just let her smell them. If all goes well maybe a few of the consent pets we talked about and tossing treats behind her. If it still goes well bring out my resident dog who she actually follows his confident/friendly lead well and let them play in yard while group stands up. I was going to a couple “test runs” with a few family members she’s doesn’t know well next week to see how it goes, but wanted to get your thoughts on this approach?Responce: Hi Kayla!That’s great to hear—congratulations! If she is consistently performing auto check-ins in distracting environments, she is ready to move to the next phase! when she does the auto check-in, say, "You are so good." (It doesn’t have to be this exact phrase, but choose a four-word phrase that’s not too long and be consistent in using it.) When she does the auto check-in, say the phrase slowly, and if, by the end of the sentence, she is still maintaining direct eye contact, you can ask her to do an easy task like touch, sit, or spin—choose something she already knows and enjoys doing. If you're unable to finish the phrase before she looks away, that’s okay! It just means you need to continue reinforcing the auto check-in a bit longer. Don’t forget to give her small treats one at a time for 5–15 seconds while you verbally praise her for the auto check-in.Regarding the meet-and-greets, doing it in your patio is a great idea! As mentioned, there’s no exact formula, and you may need to pivot depending on her body language, but your plan sounds solid. :) You might want to be prepared with a snuffle mat and consider having guests come in one at a time so it’s not overwhelming with too many new people at once. Testing out the plan with your family is an AMAZING idea!Here’s a backup plan you can also test out:Have the family already outside and place a couple of snuffle mats in different locations on your patio (not too close to the family). Let Katie May enter the patio while the family ignores her. She can explore around them, maybe sniff a little, but she also has the option to engage with the snuffle mats, alternating between checking the family out and using the mats. Once she finishes the treats on the snuffle mats, she will likely become more curious about her surroundings. You can have the family periodically move and walk to a snuffle mat and drop a treat, then come back and sit. If she starts engaging more with the family, ask them to toss a treat behind her a few times. It’s important that the toss is underhanded or done gently so the person doesn’t make any abrupt movements. If everything is still going well, I suggest removing the snuffle mats (and treats) and then letting your resident dog out. Ask the family to interact with your resident dog while still ignoring Katie May—they can practice performing consent tests with your pup while playing “hard to get” with Katie May. If she seems comfortable and starts seeking attention, then they can begin performing consent tests and interacting with her more. Keep it short and sweet. Btw, bringing your confident resident dog out is a brilliant idea, dogs can also learn through emotional contagionGood luck! Please let us know how it goes.

1/11/2025 observant. stood at front of kennel as i was cleaning and watched me. when prompted to go outside she remained unmoving, i attempted to coax her outside by moving her bed and she slightly bared her teeth and low growled - eventually went through guillotine. was easy to get her back inside, with indirect movement toward her i was able to remove/replace her food bowl and refill her water. does not potty indoors, poss. house broken. 

1/14/2025 Displaying fearful signs. Keeps eye contact when approached, but will growl and walk to back of kennel when someone gets closer. Hesitant to shift outside or come back inside after feeding/cleaning.

1/28/2025 Terrified. Fearful aggression. Very BR, barking/growling, lunging, barring teeth. 

2/2/2025 stands at front of kennel when there is commotion. observant. when approached she begins growling. will take treats tossed into kennel. when i offered a treat from my hand she continued growling and slightly bared teeth. willing to go in and out of guillotine when coaxed, but intolerant of human interaction beyond that - opened door to reduce barrier reactivity and she retreated to the corner of her run and continued growling and then chuffed a few times. kennel staff working in 200 stated they have been able to get danmooji to take treats from their hand but cannot get her to interact beyond that. behavior still fearful, quality of life appears poor.

2/16/2025 allowed me to sit in her kennel with her today. when i had my back turned to her she displayed neutral body language and stuck her neck out to sniff me (was still about 1ft away from me). would take treats when i tossed them towards her, i slowly began placing the treats closer and closer to me, eventually placing a treat next to my leg. she slowly approached to take the treat and then stepped back while maintaining neutral body language. in the afternoon i was able to place her food in front of her without reaction. she laid at the front of her kennel with her paws extended out from underneath her kennel door and watched me as i cleaned the neighboring kennels. when i opened her guillotine she displayed a slight wagging tail before exiting. came inside without issue and again displayed a slight wagging tail.  

2/18/2025 Moved Danmooji to the other side of the guillotine door where it was quieter outside.  She barked at us and moved to the back of the kennel and then we showed him a leash and asked if she wanted to go outside.  She seemed conflicted going towards the open door towards the leash and then circled back to the kennel.  Slipped an open leash over her head and let out of her kennel.  She immediately went potty, a lot.  She seemed interested in passing dogs and nervous when other pups barked or she heard noises that were loud.  When re-kenneling had to use a hook to retrieve leash. She did bit the hook.

2/23/2025 when showing the leash to her, she became avoidant and would look back and forth between the guillotine and my leash. allowed me to leash but was jumpy when it touched her. as we spent time in the yard she slowly began showing interest in me, coming up to sniff me and lick my hand. tolerant of petting on her neck and head but didn't over-indulge. when i called her to me she'd trot toward me with a high tail and put her head in my hands. placed collar on her - better response to leashing when it was clipped and unclipped to her collar.

9/27/2023 This boy needs a new name. Calm in his kennel, easy to leash and walks pretty good on a leash.  Would only pull to sniff something.  He was a bit aloof in the play yard but would check in with me regularly.  Boy knows the sound of a bag of dog treats.  Likes treats and toys, he knows sit.  Some one did a bad job on his ears.

10/5/2023 This boy is easy to get out of the kennel and walks nicely on a leash.  He doesn't react to other dogs but all the hair down his back sticks straight up.  He seems to stay aware of this surroundings.  The tracks were extra busy yesterday and he watched all the trains coming and going.  He's an aloof and serious guy but has moments of pure silliness.  After I took off the leash, he picked it up and started 'walking' himself.  It was cute but he didn't want to let go.  Eventually, he did trade for a treat and a rope toy.  There was a minute of leash biting as we got ready to go inside.  It was more playing than OA, and once he realized it wasn't play time he stopped. My favorite moment with him yesterday was him sitting on my lap, watching the train go by while I rubbed his back.  He seemed so content and relaxed.  Before returning to his kennel, I quickly washed poop off his back side.  He was calm and accommodation in the tub

10/7/2023 !!! Runny poops Sweet pup. Easy on leash. Chill

10/30/2023 Just the most chill dog ever and so grateful to get out.  He's easy out and on the leash.   He peep and pooped as soon as we got outside.  He was happy, if not a little shy to meet Lisa.  Best part there was a very reactive/aggressive dog in the next play yard (someone was trying to drop it off), Jaws totally ignored it.  His fur down the middle of his back but he didn't react at all.  Before we went back he grabbed the leash and played a game but was never aggressive or RG behavior.   Once the game was over, he walked back in calmly to his kennel.

11/4/2023 The boy is not scared of cars.  While taking him out I need to get more treats from my car, sweet boy jump right in and sat in the passenger's seat.  Broke my heart to make him get out.  We took a walk, still has some runny poos.  He did a lot more sniffing than usual but once I sat down in the play yard he climbed right into my lap.  He also spent time playing with stuffies and my leash.  What I thought was leash biting is really just him playing.  I left my leash on the table, he climb on the table and took it.  He was so proud of his find.

11/16/2023 He latched onto the water hose while Aislynn was trying to fill his water bucket. We had to use a bite stick to get it away from him. After that he latched onto someone's leash and had to use a bite stick again. Ashley had no issue leashing and moving him from J the next day. Moved to D as a precaution

11/19/2023 Was able to leash also didnt have water hose around per Jessica P-   TS

12/3/2023  No issues leashing walked easily out of the kennel.  Spent some time sniffing around the play yard.  He did try to climb on me but listened when I told him no.No resource guarding when it came to the ball would gladly drop it for a treat. However, he does have a fixation with the leash/ropes.  He tried everything to get at the leash, hanging on the gate.  We worked on leave it, eventually he got bored and went back to the ball.  Once it was time to go back, he grabbed the leash when I put it on him.  I dropped it and walked away.  He followed me, with the leash in his mouth. I feel it's a game for him.  And when you won't play he gets bored.  We walked back to the run, leash in mouth but no buying or pulling.  Once in the run, he dropped the leash for a treat.  

1/10/2024 Easily leashed and retrieved. Excited to get outside, and was patient getting into the play yard. In the play yard, Jaws sniffed around for a few minutes, un phased by my presence , occasionally taking treats. Once he was satisfied with sniffing, he became very playful and affectionate. He's an expert at leaning into pets. Takes treats very gently. Easily re-leashed, re-kenneled and unleashed. 

1/16/2024 Jaws (he really needs a new name)Visited with Jaws today.  He met me at his kennel door, I gave him a treat before attempting to take him out. He took the treat gently.   I was able to leash him easily  and walked outside with no negative behaviors.   He pulls more than I remember but he hasn't been out much.  He peed as soon as we got outside and spent a lot of time, sniffing the grass and his surroundings.   He then went to a play yard, he explored for awhile and would check in with me regularly and was very eager to take treats.  I brought out a ball, he was happy to chase and fetch.  He would drop the ball upon return.  There was no resource guarding.   He also ignored my leash.  The only time he grabbed my leash was when it was time to return to his kennel.   He held it, softly in his mouth, no pulling or biting, just holding.  He dropped it before we got to his kennel.  He went into his kennel easily and no trouble taking the leash off.He enjoyed pets, there were no body handling issues and there was no intensity in any of his action.  He was a really good boy!!

I am sorry that I did not get the volunteers' names.  Both were white girls.  One was the same person who was in the exam room when I brought CP in on Sunday-- she has long, curly, light brown hair and was wearing tall rubber boots.  And the other volunteer that I spoke with has multiple piercings, light brown hair and a shag haircut and glasses.  Both girls were very knowledgable and professional-- took the time to speak to me at length.Here's a summary of what I told them.  Some of this did not seem to be in the record, but perhaps should be:- I called Fulton County Animal Control around 6pm on Wednesday 9/25 to report a dog barking and wimpering that was tied to a fence.  It is a wooden fence that surrounds apartments (The Grant, owned by Braden Fellman) that are behind my house.  - I didn't know it at the time, but a female tenant of the apartments had also called Animal Control to report the same dog that day- Thursday morning (9/26), Animal Control had still not shown up yet, so I went over to the apartments to investigate more closely myself. By chance, I met the lady who had also called animal control in the yard of the apartments and we both walked more closely to the barking dog to see what its condition was- there were about 3 men across from the dog, outside of the apartments.  I asked them if anyone owned the dog.  They all said no, didn't know who owned it.  -CP was barking and straining on the leash tied to the fence and seemed upset.  I suggested we wait for Animal Control and not approach the dog.  One of the men decided to walk over and undo CP's leash from the fence.  I thought this was brave.  CP seemed to want to go toward his apartment (I didn't think much about this at the time).  But, he handed the leash to me.  I was surprised and the details are a little blurry.  He asked me what I was going to do with the dog.  I said I was going to take her to the shelter and maybe foster it--  I took the leash and walked her back to my house. -Animal Control showed up later that morning, and the female tenant that I had met in the yard directed the AC agent to my house to see/record the dog.-I told animal control not to take the dog because I would take it to Lifeline and potentially try to foster it.  The animal control person entered the dog into the system as "Miracle."- I also told the volunteers about the party/shooting/potential link to party host's eviction/dog-handoff that my have happened to CP before I got her and brought her to Lifeline (noted in my initial email to you).I think that pretty much covers all that I know.  I hope it helps provide more context, better records, and explain her behavior.  I also showed the volunteers the photos and videos of CP contentedly gnawing on a bone, being obedient (she seemed like she knows "sit" and "come"), and going for a  walk calmly during the time that I had her.  She also enjoyed her shoulders being rubbed. Thanks again for your time here and for taking the time to capture this dog's story accurately. I gave one of the volunteers tonight my phone #, email contact, and address, in case you have any further questions about this or need more details.  I'll still plan to follow up on Wednesday to check in..  Hopefully CP is calming down.Thank you kindly,Jami

10/1/2024 From Foster:  Good morning,I’m following up on the behavior consult we signed up for in regards to Marvelous Mary’s reactivity to men. Our previous one got canceled due to storm preparations at the old shelter so I rescheduled for 9:30am today. Not sure if maybe it got missed but I didn’t get a call and I wanted to stress the importance of addressing this issue below, with the hopes of getting the needed advice/help.While she is a wonderful dog to me and my wife, and frankly great with any of our female friends and children, she is unpredictable around men. She lives in a female only household so this is not cause for concern at home. However, when we visited my parents-in-law there were a couple of instances, alongside a most recent instance, where she was completely fine one minute and then the next she snapped.The first instance where we determined she didn’t like men was when she was outside on a leash and my uncle, a potential adopter who wanted to meet her, tried to come near her. She was good for about 10 seconds, wagging her tail, being sweet, and then just started barking at him and trying to get close to him. He is older so she wasn’t able to get near him to do anything, and we thought maybe because he is so tall and had a long beard and a hat that she just didn't like that?*The next instance was when we had her meet the rest of the family, my nephews (3 and 12), my sister in law (20) and my brother in law (21), my mother in law (55) and my father in law (54). I was right next to her tied to a tree for that first encounter. We warned my brother in law that we don’t think she likes men and to be careful. To our initial surprise, she was completely fine, let him walk her around, allowed him to give her treats and pet her, and it was a non issue. She was great with the two kids, although backing away/skittish if they were screaming. Also great with my sister and mother in law (she doesn’t really like dogs but was convinced by Mary’s cuteness and general behavior inside the house). *So 30 minutes pass by and we’re all in the living room except for my brother in law. He walks past us/Mary, also wearing a hat and having a beard, and Mary jumps up, stalks him for a second, and then tries to nip the back of his leg. He jumps and we immediately recall her, which she comes without fuss. From then I had her on leash inside and I was a little stressed/nervous about the situation so I took her outside. *Again I tied her to the same tree (me sitting by her) by the garage where people would walk by. My brother in law was going to his car and she completely loses it with him going by. Barking aggressively no matter how far/close he was to her. Time passes by, all the women and kids are fine to touch her/get close to her, she's wagging her tail as I pet her. I told my brother in law to get a spoon with peanut butter on it. Maybe we can get her to be desensitized to the fact that he is a man and being friendly can be rewarding! Albeit we only practiced for 15 minutes before we had to leave, it seemed promising for a second. I tried to have him stay seated, us getting closer to him and the treat, redirecting Mary's attention each time we sat after getting closer. There were a couple instances she barked and paid close attention to him, and then eventually happily took the peanut butter, but once he re-centered her focus, the peanut butter did not matter one bit. I was holding her on the leash but she tried to lunge at him again, barking non-stop until he was out of sight. **The big instance was my father in law. Granted we warned him not to get too close to her because of the issues with males, but nevertheless he stuck the back of his hand out for her to sniff (I was still trying to be cautious and hold her back), but sure enough she lunged at him and barked aggressively as I pulled her away to keep her from everyone. She had nipped him, superficially, but got some skin. He was fine and got the necessary care (mad/upset in the moment but he understood that she had some issues), but had this been a member of the public and someone we didn't know, it would not have been 'fine' and Mary may not have had another chance.After profusely apologizing on her behalf, I was so sad and defeated at that moment from all the culminating events. I knew she needed help to address her triggers and trauma because this behavior was unacceptable, and I was equally sad that whatever the instance was, that she had suffered/endured pain at the hands of a man who has now instilled this response in her... ***On walks I try to redirect her attention away from males or switch directions. Sometimes she catches on though or passing a man is unavoidable, in this case, she will pull on her leash and bark at them, never close enough to get to the public. I've worked on saying no, her name, go, she is great with those commands but once we come into male contact she is far less receptive to those words without a tug on her leash. I had also initially thought she was dog reactive. And while there can be some dogs she barks at, even with a female handler, she has had really positive experiences being excited to meet other dogs, and especially with an older, very well-trained/behaved pit-mix that belongs to the upstairs neighbor. They sniff each other, wag their tails happily, neither bark at each other, looking forward to seeing her when she passes by our window/porch - Mary seems to know to respect the dog rules between them. Even when in contact with the male owner (40's), Mary didn't seem to have an issue (perhaps because the other dog was protecting him and she knew to back off). ****Yesterday we were returning from a walk around our apartment complex and we encountered this same neighbor and his dog. The dogs were happy to see each other and even the owner of the other dog was able to pet Mary/touch her snout, without issue. We spent 20 minutes talking, describing Mary's history, asking for advice since his dog was also a pit-mix that he rescued some years ago from the shelter. There was one instance she tried to bark but she stopped almost immediately when we said no. He was able to touch her again, it told her to sit - she sat. Then as they were leaving and he passed us between two cars, Mary tried to go at him and barked, she didn't get near him as I had a tight grip but then we started thinking maybe she is especially triggered when she feels cornered/in a tight space with a man... ****We talked for another 5 minutes. At this time we were still around him (and his dog), and Mary was back to being a 'good girl' again. One final time the other owner tried to let her sniff the back of his hand to show her it was all okay, and she lunged and tried to nip at him. She did not break skin or anything like that, but did nose his hand like she was trying to bite. He said in this time he noticed her eyes go from normal to a trance-like state, like she wasn't really all there and the trauma was just flooding back to her to cause her to suddenly snap. Unlike the other instances with my family, she did not continue barking in his presence for the few moments we stayed to say goodbye. Again, I'm not sure if it was because his dog was right nearby to protect him, or she trusted him/believed he wouldn't hurt her on the whole, except for the brief trance-like moments where she completely forgot that he was 'nice'.Returning home, she knew she had been in the wrong. Even if I didn't put her in her crate or even get mad at her, she chose to send herself to the crate with her sad puppy eyes, I couldn't get her to come out for 10 minutes until finally my pats on the ground asking her to come sit by me and high-pitched calls had convinced her it was okay. We had a heart-to-heart as I cuddled her and spoke to her like a child (even though I know she didn't understand the words, she understood feelings). I have done everything to show her she lives in a safe environment and even people she doesn't know are not harmful. This is the one thing that is an 'issue', she is genuinely such a loveable, sweet, cuddly, cute, well-behaved (outside of these circumstances) pup that would do great in a home. I was also told she was in a foster home with all males for a moment and they did not have any issues so I'm just pulling my hair trying to understand what is going on! She would be an amazing addition to anyone's family, as soon as this male-reactivity is worked on. Otherwise, her future-homes are limited to women/children, and at all-time low adoption rates already, this is not exactly promising... I have also been trying to do research on how to overcome male-reactivity but there are no concrete answers. What I may think is a good plan of action may just be misinformation online like using a muzzle when near men (would this be a good way to work with her - the internet seems to think so to prevent bites). That is why I desperately need to get in contact with the behavior consult team and see what we can try to do. I want to do my best for her and not give up on her, but this issue cannot be left unresolved or at least not left alone without exploring different options/avenues.Feel free to contact me back at this email or at 404-663-9659.I hope to hear back as soon as possible,Guste (Marvelous Mary's Foster).  From phone consult:  We talked about reactivity to men or stranger danger:Begin muzzle training:  Muzzleupproject.comYou can pick up a muzzle from us for Marvelous Mary.  Looping in Kris, as well, that may be able to offer additional advice and experience for Marvelous Mary.

It was suggested that she would do better in a quiet place so I set a run up for her in 79. I went to grab her out of the crate with supervisor Shelby and immediately she was growling. I unlocked the door to her crate and she backed all the way up with low growls. Shelby walked by to try to coax her out and she was hard-staring and whale-eyeing her. Shelby thought it best to leave the room as Lady has a better reaction to me trying to coax her out. I was able to get my leash around her neck and get her out of the crate. Shelby walked behind me as an extra layer of protection for me and the dog. I was able to walk her to 79 with no problems, she even wagged her tail at me a few times. I got her into the kennel and got the leash of no problems. The days following this encounter I would walk by her kennel and say Hi on the daily. She was always excited to see me. She would get off her bed, wag her tail and approach the door for pets. On 12/8: I was called upon by a kennel tech because her partner was having problems getting the leash off of lady in the yard. I walked into the courtyard with her and she immediately greeted me with a tail wagging. She sat next to me as I bent down and allowed me to pet her. She seems very comfy with me and trusting of me. I was able to get the leash off and gave it back to the kennel tech. I told the tech to let me know when he needed her brought back in and I would come get her. I brought her back in after her run was cleaned and she allowed me to leash her without problems and place her back in her run without any problems. I then had to move her to clear out room 79. I got an in/out ready for her as I know people were having trouble managing her. I walked her to the run and it wasn't ready yet, I walked her to the desk and she sat under the desk by my feet until her run was ready. She allowed me to pet her and she seeked  comfort knowing I was there. Many people walked by her, she did not growl or show any signs of aggression. She is very shy/fearful but I believe with time, with the same person she will open up.

Foster/Home Notes: 10/2/2024 MARVIN – Foster Notes 9/25 General Personality Playful, friendly, laid-back, loves toys!Daily Routine I let him out of the crate around 8 am and take him and my other dog outside to go potty and play a bit. I am trying to get him on a twice-a-day feeding schedule but he is more of a grazer. I fill up his food bowl and make sure he has access to it for at least two hours in the morning (my other dog is food aggressive so I keep her in a separate area during this time). Marvin is good about not going potty in the house but he needs very frequent potty breaks or else he will pop a squat and pee. I take him outside to potty at least every two hours (often more frequent) during the day. We are still working on leash walking, so we practice that in our backyard. After a few hours of letting Marvin graze, I will let my other dog out so that they can play. I let them play and then tire themselves out. I separate them when they start getting cranky or tired. I put Marvin's food out when my other dog is put up. I basically repeat this until it's time for bed around 9 or 10pm. I put him in his crate with a full food bowl and a water bowl. Most mornings there is still a bit of food left over.What food do they eat? Purina ONE Natural SmartBlend Lamb & Rice Formula Dry Dog FoodWhat would be an ideal home and family for your foster? He would do well in a home with another dog, but would be fine on his own too. He'd ideally be with someone who understands that even though he is 5 years old, he still has some puppy-like mannerisms (mouthy-ness, destructive chewing, needs frequent potty breaks). His ideal family would work with him on these things and not get frustrated with him. He loves people and wants nothing more than to follow you around the house and chill with you on the couch. 4/2/2024 Spoke with foster Ashley about tips to socialize Tiny safely.  Here is recap. Go slow.  If you put it on and she fights it, take it off quickly and slowly build up.  Some don’t mind it, others may take more time to adjust.  Socialize her when you can.  I like small pet stores and Home Depot plant nursery when they aren’t busy.  Tell people you are in training.  If you have a patient adult, give them a few treats to toss to her.  If she takes them great.  Either way, thank them and turn around and walk the other way. I have a great pet supermarket. First we’d just go in and walk the store and leave.  Then give staff a small bag of treats to toss.  They typically understand your goal is to socialize. Invite a few friends over.  Have them stand in a circle, line or whatever space allows.  Have them toss treats. Don’t look at her, talk to her, face sideways vs directly looking at her.  Sometimes that can make a pup nervous and can cause reactions. Over time, build up and see if she will take treats from them but not in same session.  If you have people over and can, gate her away but let her see / hear what’s going on.  If she hangs out at gate, have them toss her treats.  Over time, if she wants to join, let her do that but help her on a leash so you can move her if needed. Let her decide if she wants to engage.  Also sent body language docs and body language ladder.  cheryl Scheck

He pulled the leash all the way to the office but was otherwise easily handled, no leash biting observed. In the office, he ran around in circles and sniffed different areas. I pulled out some treats and he immediately led into a sit when asked. He is very food motivated and was easily taught "wait". I started teaching him hand signs with sit and wait, repeating "sit" while placing my hand open palm in a "stop" signal until he would sit and wait without the verbal command (only took about 5 minutes for him to learn this). He's very young and clearly frustrated that he is not more active. A bit of a velcro dog, followed Stephanie around the office constantly. He does jump but easily redirected by turning your back and giving the "stop" hand signal. Practiced leashing and unleashing a few times and he did not attempt to bite the leash. I didn't observe any leash biting at any point in our leash interactions or any particularly concerning OA but he is visibly frustrated, very easily redirected with hand signals or command. Overall, he appears to be an under stimulated puppy with a lot of stored energy that is relatively easily quelled with command training. He settled pretty quickly on his own in the office after about 15 minutes of alternating command training an ignoring him. Recommending level is altered from L2-OA/LB to L1.  Status Change: Moved from L2-OA/LB to L1.

"Dog Test" Notes: 9/11/2024 Personality: A little to himself at first. Doesn’t like fast movements when going to pet him. When we did our walk he barely paid me any attention. After some time he finally took a treat from me. After doing his dog testing we hung out in a play yard for a little. I let him come up to me on his own time. After feeling comfortable with me he allowed me to pet him, slowly, and finally gave me some gentle kisses. Dog Test 1: Anastasia (F) met through the fence, he had slow tail wags and hackles up but was whining to get to her. Once she came out of the play yard, Kroger was eager to meet her. We did a side by side walk and let them interact. You can tell he wanted to play but still had hackles up. Tail was wagging the whole time, was play bowing and sniffing her back side a lot. You could tell they wanted to play with each other. Dog Test 2: Dottie (F) Kroger was in the play yard and Dottie approached, she is so sweet was giving him kisses. He really liked her a lot, had his tail wagging, still had his hackles up but body was relaxed. Came out of the play yard to do a face to face, she was so sweet trying to kiss him. He tried playing with her and I think he was a little too much for her at one point because she let out some scared pee. We gave her a moment and then tried to let them sniff each other again and she seemed a little more relaxed that go around. Dog Test 3: Trevor (M) They didn’t seem very interested in each other in the play yard. They did a brief sniff and went their own way after. Took him out of the play yard and they were a little standoffish towards each other at first. Kroger kept wanting to sniff Trevors behind and Trevor was ok with allowing him to do it. They weren’t overly interested in each other and were perfectly fine coexisting. Medical: 53lbs, HW-, 2 years old,How Do I Handle Stress? Not doing the best in kennel, jumping really high when approaching his kennel. Walks ok throughout the building. Didn’t want to go back into his kennel. What Do I Need Help With Most? Being more socialized. A little weird with being touched at first. The Most Memorable Thing About Me: Once he finally relaxed around me and gave me the sweetest kisses. You can tell he is just not used to getting a lot of love. Intake Info: ACO pickup at a Krogers. Was found wondering around in the parking lot for a few days. What is my strategic out? Dog friendly, not very big, sweet boy. Ongoing care: Socializing him with people. Other notes: Overall really sweet, takes treats gently, doesn’t know any commands. Just go slow when giving him pets and attention. Don’t go over his head to pet him.

Foster/Home Notes: 7/29/2024 Things are going great with Juliette! She has become much more comfortable with our resident dog and with our house. Medical: I came in last Wednesday to get antibiotics because she had a pretty bad upper respiratory infection/cold (not kennel cough I don’t think) but after the past few days on meds, she is feeling 1000x better and she’s like a new dog! She’s a little underweight, but we are feeding her plenty to make up for it :) Behavioral: We did a very slow introduction to my resident dog, who is a little reactive, so I’m familiar with proper dog introductions because of that. They are now doing great and walk well together, sit on the couch together, and walk around the back yard together sniffing things. They haven’t engaged in play much - I don’t know that Juliette really knows how to play?? She likes toys and bones, but doesn’t seem to know play cues with other dogs and mine probably isn’t the best to learn from because she has her own issues! Otherwise, meeting dogs should be a bit slower and proper (parallel walks, not nose to nose) and she will do fine with that. You can tell she likes being around other dogs, but needs proper introductions and slow. My dog doesn’t like to share, but they have come a LONG way and now they have been respectful of each other’s toys and space!Other notes:- she doesn’t chew on anything - she is completely potty trained- she is fine going in the crate, but doesn’t LOVE it - she sleeps through the night in her bed- she is VERY affectionate and loves people- she is fairly well trained and knows “sit” and “down” and we have been working on “stay” and she is doing GREAT!- she has low/medium energy - doesn’t run around the house but likes going on walks and playing with toys or chewing bones - then is very happy cuddling up next to her people- she’s incredibly sweet and loving! - would make an AMAZING pet and someone will be soooo lucky to have her- I will send more pictures to the email you provided! I think she would do well in a house with another dog who is super chill and submissive dog (to avoid any issues) because she enjoys the company of another dog but would also be fine with her humans.

10/1/2024 Stunner stayed in our home for 6 days, he was great the entire time.We went to restaurants, evening at an outside bar with music, the outlets and Home Depot. Hedid great in all those settings. He would people watch but was not anxious or vocal. No issues with resource guarding.He responds well to “no” as this was used when he was using his mouth too hard. He did fine ina crate and took very little time to get used to it. He is smart and picks up tasks quickly.Stunner is active and will run and fetch, although he is more interested in tug-o-war thandropping the object, but again, this would be an easy behavior to modify. He was just ascontent to sit in our lap or lay down under my desk while working from home. He enjoyed allkinds of squeaky toys and preferred a dog bed most of the time. He had a few accidents but atthis point he is close to potty trained…I say that knowing it will revert as it usually does in ashelter but the behavior is there so a new family should be able to accomplish potty trainingfairly quickly.From what I saw he was exceptionally good at dealing with any type of anxiety, he would “shakeit off” with a full body shake. He did this several times in the car when we left the shelter, heseemed unsure but was always compliant and responsive. When we did something new withhim, he was apprehensive but responded to encouragement, he would shake and then continuewith what we were doing. For instance, he was not accustomed to stairs, within 2 days he wasable to go up and down the “open view” stairs. Basement stairs that had walls was a little morestressful, but in a few more days he was able to overcome that fear and was able to go up anddown any set of stairs.
