5/23/2024 Personality: Irish is a very sweet girl. She loves cuddling up in your lap, giving and receiving affection. A little shy but can warm up once she gets comfortable.  Dog Test 1: First dog test we did with a larger female dog. Irish was not comfortable, she was full hackles with a stiff tail.  She started growling at the other dog we were testing with inside the fence. We did not do a side by side walk because we didn’t want to further stress Irish out. Dog Test 2: We then had the idea to try a smaller dog so we found a a male puppy. She did a lot better with the puppy. We let them sniff through the fence first and then allowed them into the same play yard together. The puppy was interested in her but was really engaged. Once we let them into the play yard together, both still on leash, we allowed the puppy to slowly sniff Irish. Irish was still a little nervous but allowed the puppy to sniff her. Over time you could tell Irish was getting more relaxed having the puppy around. Medical:How Do I Handle Stress? Not well, she was biting on the guillotine door and I requested she be moved to a different kennel. What Do I Need Help With Most? Not feeling as nervous, getting out on more walks. The Most Memorable Thing About Me: How affectionate and sweet she is. Intake Info: She was seen being put out of a car and abandoned. What is my strategic out? Size and how affectionate she is. Ongoing care: Interacting with more dogs. Other notes: Irish would do best with smaller, low energy dogs. She will need really slow intros when introducing to another pet. She would not mind be the only dog in the home. 

6/22/2024 Irish was introduced to Onion (F) in the multi purpose room. We kept them on leash and let them walk around the room before introducing them. Irish was fixated at first on Onion but once we walked around more she got more comfortable with her being in the room. We did slow intros and allowed them to meet briefly and then separated. Irish was a little stiff at first but then her tail started wagging and you could see her opening up more as time went on. They were able to interact (still on leash) and Irish actually gave Onion some kisses at one point. This was a big step for Irish and I think she would be ok with another dog with the correct intro and with time. She probably wouldn’t like a dog much bigger than her and definitely someone more on the calmer side. But overall she made a big step with this dog test and she did really good. By the end of the test she was relaxed, walking around the room, interacting with Onion with no issues.

11/9/2023 From owner:I wanted to give a little more context to Noodles' "bite incidents" because I don't feel like I explained them well enough on the questionnaire and it matters.   The cat incident is the reason our landlord forced us to return her. We own our home but he owns the community/land. We were allowed to have pets but as the community landlord he reserved the right to impose new restrictions at any point, which is what he did: said she has to go and now banned pitbulls. Our family & friends live in Oregon/Hawaii and we didn't have anyone able to take her.   The cat incident: the community has a dog park, and while we were playing fetch, our neighbor's cats leapt inside and ran straight at my dog to fight. My dog was in the middle of chasing a ball when the cat landed on her face, and so she bit the cat. As you can see by the current state of Noodles' face, she was also hurt by the cat. It was traumatic to witness and I thought the cat was going to die due to the bite/bloodloss, but I got word from my neighbor that the cat eventually came home and the vet prescribed antibiotics and the cat will be okay.   So, the cat will be fine and honestly I believe the cat was the instigator. This same cat has run up to her before on walks, and while Noodles looked interested in engaging, I was always able to tug my dog away and everything was fine. This incident was a perfect storm of the cat jumping on a dog who was in her "happy play place" where she chases & chews on balls.   Secondly, with the man's hand: I did mention in the questionnaire that she shows a little fear reactivity towards people when a stranger comes up and pets her. I believe part of this is the context of our environment. We're in a very small rural forest community where we only have 10 residents. When we were in the city on a handful of occasions, she did not show reactivity towards people. For the most part, if we ran into people in our little piece of the woods, she would either bark, or ignore them. We don't know her past so we just asked people not to pet her, but when a large man came up and pet her anyways, that's when she jumped up and was barking at him, and we saw her mouth go to his hand. He didn't bleed, and didn't mention it. It was easy to tug her away from him and have her settle down next to us. We asked if he was okay and he said he was fine. So I just wanted to give context for this "bite incident" where technically her mouth grazed a man's hand but it was not a serious bite or wound situation.   I am not sure how she would do with other dogs, but her prey drive would not do good in a house with cats. I think she would be an awesome friend for *older* children, because her high velocity excited tail might push down a small child.    I hope this info helps anyone who inquires about Noodles but is hesitant hearing she has a "history." She is a truly sweet soul, full of joy, and incredibly loyal to her people. Not for one second do I believe she would do anything to harm the humans she knows. If we weren't only in year 2 of a 5 year lease, we would be looking for a way to move and keep her. I know you guys are so busy, thank you guys for taking her in, hopefully her previous foster is available, she seemed fond of Noodles.

7/12/2024 Today we wanted to discuss Leash Reactivity, and potty training:There are two main reasons why dogs display leash reactivity: fear or frustration. A fearful dog wants to get away from the thing he’s afraid of, so he displays distance-increasing body language, such as snarling and growling. It’s his way of saying, “Hey, you! You make me uncomfortable! Stay away from me!” A frustrated dog, on the other hand, displays distance decreasing body language, such as playful barking and bounciness. It’s his way of saying, “Hey, you look fun! Come meet me!”The first step in working with your dog’s reactivity is to determine the underlying cause behind the behavior through his body language. Is he fearful or frustrated? The answer to that question can shape the behavior modification approach you use.Threshold resource attached. We walked to the lobby with the female adopter first and a man who was standing nearby in the lobby tried to reach over and pet Pharadise but she ducked and side eyed him. He didn’t understand her body language snd reached to pet her while she was trying to walk away from him and she tucked her butt away and turned around to stare at him. I distracted her by talking to her and continued walking. She was really friendly and eagerly solicited attention from me and the woman. We went into the yard and she was perfect. Immediately rolled over for belly rubs and loved all the attention she was getting from me and the female adopter (the man she was with was in the car with her resident car). Kate came in and Pharadise had zero issues with her coming in and playing with her. The woman went to go get her friend and her dog. Pharadise sniffed her dog well through the fence but then lunged at the fence when the man came up behind the woman. I asked if the man could come into the yard before we started the meet and greet to determine if she was going to be okay with him. She was originally panting from the heat but switched to a stress pant and worried eyebrows. She walked with me on leash by him a few times and she completely ignored him, turning her back to him and trying to avoid making contact with him. I asked him to approach her carefully and she continued to ignore him. He reached out slowly to pet her and she sniffed his hand, licked his fingers briefly before stiffening. I pulled the leash back at the same time she started alarm barking at him. We determined it wasn’t a good fit and did not continue with the dog test. There were two women yelling in the hallway about how cute a dog was when we were coming back in, spooking Pharadise and causing her to back up and alarm bark at them when they tried to rush and pet her. I advised she was nervous and they understood and stepped back. There was also a man standing behind them. I walked her into the 80s and Lamar was standing nearby. I tried to tell him to give me some space to put her back but he kept approaching saying she was fine with him but each time he got closer she leaned further and further away, her eyes getting wider. He wasn’t picking up on her body language so I stepped between her and him and told him to please give  her time to decompress. I’m not sure if she actually is okay being handled by him or just tolerates it. He came behind while I was unleashing her and she low growled. Pharadise has some minimal general anxiety but clearly has some aversion/distrust of men. (Could be contributed to 2/3 men not recognizing her signs of stress and continuing to try and interact with her).

He loves meeting all people. - Tres should not be placed with cats (too much interest... maybe I'm wrong, but I don't think so). - Thres should not be rehomed with children.  - He loves children, but he does enough resource guarding to make that an unsafe option in my opinion. They then let Smiley go in first, then had each person go in quietly one at a time.  Smiley stayed settled and relaxed and didn’t even need to go in crate.  Did also suggest they try moving crate into guest room vs living room if helpful to have him relax more if others there.  In this case, not really needed.  Advised to monitor behavior as they continue to taper traz during the transition to fluoxitine. Dr. Flowers’ tapering instructions:  Per clinic... Give 100mg of Trazadone twice a day for the next 7 days, then 50mg of Trazadone twice a day for 7 days then stop - per Flowers. Foster/Home Notes: 12/13/2023  I wanted to reach out to you about Jean. First I want to say what a sweetheart she is.  She hasn’t had an accident inside. She is soooo friendly and loves snuggles and bringing her toys to show them off when she sees us first thing. she doesn’t bark at all except when she saw one of my cats. She greeted my 13 year old son wonderfully after arriving to the house for the first time. She greeted my 11 year old daughter arriving home no problems later that evening for the first time, grabbing her plushie to show her with excitement. and she also greeted my husband this morning, who she hadn’t met yet, when he arrived home from working over night. she was excited to welcome him as a new person into the home. She won’t walk into the kitchen, she quietly stands at the entrance to the kitchen waiting. She happily eats her food without food aggression towards us if we are close.  She is gentle taking treats. Goes potty outside easily. Went to bed happily last night and after I took out to go pee around 1am, she went back to bed like she knew the routine already. She is absolutely wonderful!! 🥰  A few things that have me concerned though. It seems being in a creat aggravates her back knees. She is well behaved in a creat so that’s not an issue. But I actually have only had her in the creat a few times because of obvious discomfort when getting out even after a short time (lass than an hour), and the fact she has been great hanging out downstairs or in my son’s room when he is in there. That’s where she slept last night. I think the stairs in our house might aggravate her knees as well. I was told she needs surgery on both back knees at some point soon.  I had kept my cats in my bedroom until half way through the night. Until my older cat insisted on being let out. Simply because Jean seems to come out of her creat stiff and limping even after a short time I let her sleep uncreated. I was worried my son would walk out to go toilet during the night and she would get out and neither her nor my cats are ready to meet face to face.  my cats are not happy staying confined to my bedroom. I’ve started to leash Jean to bring her out of my sons room for potty breaks, seen my cats are back to freely moving around the house. which she is fine with, but she seems overly interested in the cats as I take her outside. Over time I’m sure this would ease off. Seen she seems in pain from being in her creat, I am not sure I feel comfortable leaving her in my son’s bedroom uncreated with the door shut without someone in there with her. This will be a problem when I need to go out and leave her home without someone here. I don’t think she Would need to be created for the most part to transition into a new home because she is so wonderful. But because of my cats I think the process is going to be difficult  with the creat and her being in pain. My older cat will transition fast, as she has been around dogs before,  but it seems the younger two are not taking it so well. It will be a longer process.  Another concern is my son was getting a rash and itching. He has asthma and has been allergy tested for dogs when he was younger and it was negative. But this seems to have changed. Our last pup was a pultipoo, so being hypoallergenic he didn’t have an issue. He takes an allergy pill every day but I had to give him Benadryl last night.  Jean is so wonderful and I know she would make a wonderful addition to a family! She is so easy to have in the home, minus the cat introduction process and her being in pain with being in a creat.

Jedi was easily leashed from his spot in the barn and started off pulling strong. I paused to harness him and he went face to face with another dog through a fence with his tail wagging. Action: Needs to be neutered and dog tested!
>Jedi dog test 7/5/23 DN/LF
When I took him out of the kennel, he was very excited and could barely wait for me to put the leash on before running to the door. He ignored every other dog that he passed. Jedi was tested with Big Boy. They met through the fence first, sniffing and wagging tails. Once in the same yard, we did a parallel walk where they both sniffed with wagging tails. Jedi was interested in interacting but wanted human attention equally as much. We then took them to a front yard where we dropped the leashes to see how they would interact. They mostly just sniffed around the yard and went potty. They also briefly interacted with a dog in the yard beside them before moving on. There were a few instances where play was briefly initiated but Jedi was defensive, giving a short growl or jumping up, which Big Boy quickly submitted too before we pulled them away for a break. Overall pretty positive. Jedi is non-reactive on leash or through a fence once outside. He could live with other dogs but may need time to get settled and gain confidence before being comfortable. Videos in Asana
Result: Positive, Jedi will be placed on the surgery schedule ASAP and then sent to a foster home

Foster’s Name: Jessica Pope
General Personality: Fred is so incredibly sweet. He's a little bit of a goofball and dying to be someone's best pal.
Daily Routine: He gets up early very easily and we go on a fairly easy but long walk, as long as the temperature is low enough. 
He wasn't particularly interested in eating at any specific times, requiring some extra snacky incentives to eat on a schedule (a bit of peanut butter or shredded cheese), so I switched to letting him free feed with my dog and have seen a lot of improvement. 
I'm generally home and working from the computer all day, so he likes to sit on the couch and snooze until I get up and it's time to follow me around. 
Most of his days are spent bringing out every single toy in the baskets to show me and then he's off to play with it or see what my dog is doing.
He goes out around 7-8 AM, 4-5 PM, and 10-11 PM to keep a semblance of a schedule in case I need to return to an office eventually.
Food: Kirkland brand beef protein
Ideal Family & Home for foster dog: Fred is pretty flexible. He could easily be an apartment/condo dog since he seems to enjoy a long walk more than playing off-leash. He would do best with another older dog to show him the ropes. Haven't seen that he's been tested with cats but I haven't seen any high-prey drive behavior. I don't know that he's currently ready to live with kids. He's just a little too enthusiastic about how hard he wants to love his people and could knock someone smaller over.
Houstrained? (Scale 1-5): 5
Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts or destruction?: Fred says "hard pass" to a crate. He's figured out how to escape it and I worry that reinforcing the crate would just lead to his getting injured during the continued escape attempts..
Where do they sleep at night?: He would very much prefer to sleep with me but I've successfully gotten to sleep on the floor. But if someone wants a snuggly bed dog, Fred is READY.
Do they sleep through the night?: Yes
Kid exposure: No
Cat exposure: No
Do they prefer men or women?: No preference
Live with another dog? Yes
Been around another dog?: He immediately took to my dog. She's a senior female that's only about 10 pounds bigger than him. He seems to prefer dogs his own size or smaller. We attempted an introduction with a much larger dog (about twice his size) and he wasn't aggressive but didn't seem comfortable.
Commands known: Sit, go lay down, off/down (he's a jumper)
Leash reactive?: It's not very consistent. He passes some dogs silently but will bark back at others that initiate the barking. He walks pretty well alongside my dog without getting tangled.
What do you use to walk your foster dog?: I had been walking him with his collar until yesterday. I was trying to restrain him and he jerked his way out of the collar. He's currently wearing a standard harness, but I'll likely get him a no-pull harness that fits a little better tomorrow.
Leash walking rating (Scale 1-5): 3
Car riding?: He does best when he's sharing the back seat with my other dog. He doesn't get any motion sickness, but will race back and forth across the back seat if he has the room. He's also figured out how to get under the backseat hammock, and seems to feel more at ease underneath it. He will jump into the back easily, but is generally desperate to get out and will launch himself HARD. We're working on it.
Baths?: He doesn't like it but is tolerant. He'll jump in himself but does need encouragement to stay in during the process.

How much exercise does it take to tire them out?: He's pretty good with a 30ish minute walk but could definitely go for longer if the weather permits.
If they don’t get exercise, what happens?: He's still pretty mellow, but you're in for some full-speed, breakneck zoomies later

Favorite toys or games: Anything that involves getting attention first and foremost. He'll chase a ball but won't bring it back yet. He loves to eviscerate a stuffed toy but knows not to eat the stuffing or squeaker.

I got him inside and let him sniff around and meet my dog, and then he ran in the bathroom and put himself in the tub. I'm not sure if he read my mind or just agreed that he was overdue, but it was a pleasant surprise!
I love my foster and think he/she is fabulous because He's just so sweet and kind. He's ready for someone to love him forever and they'll receive it back tenfold.

That said, he wasn't shaking every time he refused to walk, and it was also very cold out on our walks- I can't say with confidence that he wasn't simply cold once he stopped moving (even in his little jacket). Did see a tail tuck at times, but no pancaking, no reactivity, just refusing to walk. However, he seemed comfortable walking in some directions but not others, and could be encouraged to budge a few feet if I tossed a high-value treat down the sidewalk. The refusal to walk escalated two times and he began to bite his leash; based on his body language, he really just seemed frustrated and was trying to displace that behavior. But otherwise, when moving, I think he truly felt comfortable and wanted to be outside. So thinking it could be a bit of fear combined with some basic indifference/ stubbornness- and I'm sure the latter would be fine with a little training/ some fun walking games and treats. All this said, I did find it interesting that there was such a significant change between DFTD/ first two days of WW vs the last few days of WW. He may have just gotten more comfortable in a matter of days and his personality started to come through- definitely understand the importance of decompression and anticipate personality/ behavior fluctuations will occur! I will say that I think he could benefit immeasurably from an adoption into a family with other dog(s)- he seemed most eager to walk when there were other dogs around, and if he's having fear outside, I think a confident dog could help him when out on walks.

Bobo eats 3 meals a day to try and gain a little weight - each one about 1 cup of kibble. 

He got a steroid shot for his allergies last Friday (8/18). The shot will last one week to help stop the itching. On this Friday (8/25) he will start the steroid pills (smaller pill bottle with big white pills) to finish out the allergy treatment. He will get one every 48 hours until the bottle runs out. 

The steroids make him super thirsty and he needs to pee more often. I’ve been giving him lots of water in the morning and early afternoon and taking him out to pee every few hours. I stop giving him water around 4/5 PM and then take him out to pee right before bed. He can usually last through the night without an accident in his crate. 

Before he was on steroids, I let him sleep out in the living room, but I’ve been keeping him in the crate at night since he’s been on meds to try and make sure he doesn’t have an accident when I’m asleep. He doesn’t mind the crate once you give him a gentle push inside. 

When I’m gone, I have been leaving him to roam in my living room. He chewed up one coaster when he was feeling naughty, but otherwise he just naps or wanders around (I watch him on my doggy camera). I have been giving him a kong with peanut butter when I leave which he really loves. 

He’s learning how to use toys and go for walks, so he’s a work in progress! He doesn’t really pull on a leash - if anything I am dragging him along to stop him from sniffing so much. He probably won’t need many walks at all if you guys have a big backyard! Bobo is definitely not a high energy dog. He just needs lots of loving <3

So far, Bobo has shown 0 aggression. He does not resource guard and has been very friendly of all people and dogs we’ve met out and about. Other dogs are sometimes wary of him since he isn’t neutered, but many have warmed up to him after they realize he just wants to sniff their butt. He doesn’t hump other dogs but he does sometimes hump me, so just firmly push him off and say NO super loudly. He usually gets the picture lol. 

His neuter is on 9/7 and they want you to drop him off the night before and pick him up at the end of the day. I can help with drop off and pick up since I’m only 10 minutes away from the shelter if you need it!

He needs to be neutered ASAP so other dogs give him a chance and more people could be potential adopters/fosterers. He LOVES other dogs, they just don’t love him.

Foster/Home Notes: 12/20/2023 Foster Questionnaire 12/20/23 "Lani" Easy button, potty & crate trained, low energy, curious about dogs Foster’s Name: Mike Gardner Temp foster needs?: No, but we need to get her adopted by the first week of January General Personality: Our easiest foster yet. She LOVES her crate, lays down on car rides, is not reactive to other dogs, and loves people (including seniors and kids). She loves treats and takes them sooo gently. She almost never barks (unless she is startled). As such, her "signs" that she needs to go out are very subtle, but she has us trained now. She does not jump up on humans, which is awesome. She's a very mellow dog 95% of the time. But, she gets daily zoomies for 5 minutes in the 3pm - 5pm time slot every day, regardless of exercise. During her zoomies, she can be a little mouthy. She doesn't bite, but she wants to put her mouth on her humans. She responds to "No". This might be leftover behavior from having puppies. Daily Routine: Gets up at 6:45, pees, eats breakfast, poops, then goes back to bed. Around 9:30, she comes down and is ready for a walk She hangs out with us most of the day After lunch, we take her on another walk. At 6:30, she eats dinner She spends the evening curled up between us while we read or watch TV. At 10pm, she's ready for bed and sleeps through the night. Food: She eats two cups of kibble per day, one at 6:45am and one at 6:30pm. She watches the clock. We gave her canned dog food to take her meds, which she loves and expects. Four little meatballs after each meal. She is happy to clean a plate of human scraps, but she know that never happens until after we eat and doesn't happen every time. It is believed that she's alergic to chicken (common in PitBulls) Ideal Family & Home for foster dog: She is an indoor dog. She goes out to do her business, then is ready to come back in and be with people or go to her crate. We don't allow dogs on furniture, but she would happily get on the couch with us as she is a snuggler. Houstrained? (Scale 1-5): 5 Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts or destruction?: Yes, her crate is her favorite place (it has the most comfortable bed). She goes in voluntarily throughout the day. Where do they sleep at night?: In a crate Do they sleep through the night?: Yes Kid exposure: Kids of all ages. She loves them and they love her. She is super muscular so kids pulling on her doesn't phase her at all. Cat exposure: No cats as yet. Do they prefer men or women?: No preference Live with another dog? No Been around another dog?: She is interested in other dogs, but not obsessively. She just wants to smell them. She is not "reactive". If dogs bark at her, she just wants to move on past them. Commands known: She will sit if there is a treat involved. She will generally come and she knows "No". She is challenging to train on new tricks because she gets so excited about the treats, that she cannot concentrate. Leash reactive?: No, not at all. But, if she sees a squirell, she will try to chase it. She understands no. What do you use to walk your foster dog?: Harness and retractable leash. Leash walking rating (Scale 1-5): 4 Car riding?: She lays down immediately and stays down the entire ride. She doesn't even look out the window. Baths?: She doesn't love a bath, but she puts up with it just fine. Energy Level: 2 How much exercise does it take to tire them out?: We normally walked her about 2 miles per day, but we took her on walks of 4+ miles and she was fine. If they don’t get exercise, what happens?: She gets her zoomies regardless of exercise. But, she needs her walks or she gets excitable. A perfect day for your foster would include Sticking to her schedule. She learned ours quickly and clearly likes a routine. I think she would struggle in a home that doesn't have routines. Cuddly Level: 4 Favorite toys or games: Plain Rawhide... absolutely loves it. Tell us a funny story: When she gets up in the morning, she has a stretching routine. She does downward dog, spoots, then she pitty-pats across the room (all while expecting to be rubbed down). When she's waiting for a treat, she sits and her tail will tap, tap, tap faster and faster on the floor. It's really cute. I love my foster and think he/she is fabulous because If we were at the point in our lives for a permanent dog, she would be our foster fail. She has so many great qualities and almost none of the "doggie challenges" that we are used to in other fosters. What makes your foster nervous or unhappy?: She likes us to stick together. When one of us leaves, she waits be the door for them to return. Foster’s manners: No jumping up on people, no barking, no getting in trash, no jumping on countertops. Mouthy when she gets excited or you rub her belly, but she will stop when you say "no". Behavioral issues or quirks: She has a tendancy to poop at the bottom of our back stairs. Which requires us to keep a shovel there. Medical Issues: Not currently. Getting spayed was rough, because she had had puppies recently. She is just getting over an alergic reaction to chicken. It was causing sores between her toes. They have cleared up and we changed her food to a "non-chicken" variety of kibble and canned food. She's appears to be in amazing shape right now. Social Media presence: Facebook - 4 Instagram (posts/stories) - 1 Nextdoor - 1 Youtube - 1 Last adoption event your foster went to: n/a What prevents you from taking your foster to more adoption events: We've had a crazy busy fall. We are happy to do this after the Christmas holiday. What gear & materials do you utilize to help get your foster recognized? Word of mouth. Everyone loves her and we are constantly promoting her. We thought we had her adopted twice, but it didn't work out because of family situations, not because of her. When was the last time you took your foster out on the town?: Multiple times every day. What prevents you from taking your foster out on the town more often?: We do. What is preventing your foster from being its most adoptable self?: I don't have time to market them How can we help?: Social media partner, Getting foster to events, Gear (Adopt Me) What day do you give your foster preventatives?: 1st day of the month Are you interested in adopting your foster pet?: No Would you be willing to have your foster dog transfer to a rescue partner?: Yes, but we don't think that's necessary Any other info?: She get excited on walks when she sees a runner. We think that a previous owner might have run with her. We don't run, so we didn't test our theory.

1/2/2024 It breaks my heart to have to write this, but Rascal is not going to be a good fit for my family.  We knew going into this that his heightened arousal could be just a factor of shelter life, or potentially a longer standing behavioral issue. 12/2/2023 I fostered Brandy from Nov 28-Dec 2 at my home! Here are some notes:  she’s an incredibly cuddly dog. It took her only 30-40 minutes to settle down in my apartment before she simply laid next to me on my lap; she does this thing where she will walk back and forth over you until she rests her front legs on you and lays there; she also loves to sleep in the bed with us and even if we weren’t petting or rubbing her, she seemed to enjoy simply being next to us. Loves squeaky toys, chew toys and rope! She’d get so excited at squeaky balls and enjoyed chewing on the rope I bought her. When there’s a toy nearby, that will be her SOLE focus.  When she saw other dogs, she’d want to run towards them and she’d often whine or bark at them.  She is hard on a leash and even when you try to pull her towards you, she starts to walk on her hind legs! When she’s off the leash though, she doesn’t run away - it’s as if she trusts you as her owner, she will come when you call for her.  Clearly potty trained; she did have accidents in the home though, but it only happened when I left her alone for a few minutes to go grab the mail. I wish I had a yard I could’ve taken her to run around in because that’s what I felt she really wanted to do.  She is easy to carry and isn’t aggressive when you try to pick her up She would bark if someone was at the door When greeting someone new for the first time, she’d jump on them excitedly, it was a little overwhelming at first. Her nails are also incredibly sharp; I wasn’t able to file them, but she did leave a few scratches on my skin, especially since she’s jumpy and hyper! She likes treats and she’s ready to obey when you’ve got them in your hand! She was able to do “sit” and “jump” well, and if I had more time with her, I’m sure I could’ve taught her more because she was easy to teach and she listened and wasn’t distracted easily.  Lastly, when traveling in the car, she was restless because she kept moving back and forth.   That’s all I had for her! Wonderful dog, I hope she can get adopted into a family that has a big yard, lots of toys, and loves cuddling with their pups.

It would be best if his adopter was okay with a Gold Rush not knowing all the basic commands just yet. There was a little boy sitting in one of the chairs outside the entrance and when Gold Rush walked by him he stopped, walked up to him, put his head in the little boys lap, tail wagging, and the little boy pet him and gave him some attention. He is usually pretty calm on our walks and he walks pretty well on a leash for not having had training. He has barked at our neighbor and his dog out on a walk before, but it seems more out of excitement and curiosity rather than any sort of aggression. He also wants to run after squirrels sometimes. He is pretty easy to redirect, either by walking the other way while directing him verbally or with high value treats. What devices do you use to walk your dog? Twiggie is very good at keep away though so he is often chasing her for a toy but it is cute to watch them chase each other. Tell us a fun story about your foster... One of the first nights we had him at home he curled up on the couch with us for the first time and fell asleep. Behavior Notes: 12/15/2023 Very S/F. She looked very sad in her pin, and hadn’t touched her food. She didn’t have any notes or pictures so I decided to take her out and get to know her/get more content. She was very hard to leash in her pin but was willing to come out once she was leashed and was excited and tail wagging to go with me while still being skittish. Once we got out to the play yard I had been talking to her sweet but she only responded with giving me a little side eye. I decided to keep the leash on her bc I was unsure about reaching at her face with her looking at me like this and how hard it was getting her leashed in the first place. In the play yard she wasn’t interested at all in treats or toys. Once I tried dropping the leash and this is when she got the most scared, with the leash laying on the ground beside her she froze in fear for a good minute until I maneuvered beside her, not facing her, to bend down and grab the leash without intimidating her. After I picked up the leash and called her to walk with me she was okay again. Mostly wanted to stare out in the woods. After being in the play yard I took her over into the grassy area to walk a bit and this did excite her the most, she wanted to eat the grass as well. Since she got a little pep in her step while in the grass I bent down to see if I could solicit pets but she again gave me side eye and let me know she was uncomfortable with me in her space. I got I few pets in on her back but could tell she wasn’t enjoying it so not much else. When I took her back to her pin, again she was very afraid of the leash. Leashing seems to be the thing that makes her most uncomfortable. I can tell she is a sweet girl just very terrified at the moment and seems like she just needs someone to help tell her she is safe so her sweet playful personality can come out. She doesn’t seem mean AT ALL, just very very scared and unsure.

Re: Anna (as known to FCAS, and "Dot" as we were calling her). 

We fostered and adopted Dot over the course of a month. She has many positive traits and was generally a joy to have in our home. My husband and I work from home so we had lots of time with Dot during the month.

During our fostering, Dot and our older male dog showed some aggressive behavior towards each other over food. We were able to address this during our fostering period and felt that we had this managed well enough to adopt her. However, in the past week there were two incidents which occurred in which Dot became aggressive towards our other dogs (both our male and female dog). The first incident was when Dot seemingly became jealous of our female lab being brushed by my husband, as I brushed Dot. Dot put her head on my husband's shoulder and then jumped off the sofa onto our Lab and caused a fight. The second incident took place the day we surrendered Dot. Dot saw someone walking outside on the sidewalk through a window, began to bark and then got into a fight with our male dog who barked back at her. I was bitten in several places in the process of trying to separate them. 

Dot was gentle around us otherwise. We have two young kids and other than when these incidents occurred, she was good around them. She is generally high energy and was happy to see us. She played well in the yard and was learning commands. She loves to be a big lap dog and wants as much attention as possible but will also roll around on the rug, entertain herself, or lay on the sofa contentedly. She is a strong chewer (can rip a tennis ball or toy easily) and is a quick eater (we used a slow feeding bowl) and would jump up on the counter/table for food, but was learning not to do so. She liked to play fetch and was starting to drop the toy and understand the game better. She crates well and would not bark in the crate unless she heard noises. While not fully house trained, she was making great strides.

We have lots of photos we can send, if those would be helpful. Please let us know. We hope she can find the right home.
